speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The purpose of my speech is, however, not to deliver a lesson in biology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The purpose is to outline the consequences that menopause and perimenopause can have on women, and to suggest some strategies to enable our existing systems to more effectively respond to these consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Some of you may recall that earlier this year I spoke in Parliament about the importance of building a culture of gender equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In my speech today, I will continue this theme and will discuss the disproportionate impact that menopause and perimenopause have on women and the importance of applying a gender informed approach to better understand and remedy this imbalance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am also the President of the Singapore Muslim Women’s Association, or PPIS; a non-profit organisation focused on women empowerment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Notably, PPIS is part of the Singapore Alliance for Women in Ageing (SAWA), together with Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE), the Singapore Council of Women’s Organisations (SCWO) and the Tsao Foundation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am doing so not on the assumption that people are unfamiliar with the terms I will be using, but because it is important that we have a common understanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Menopause refers to a woman’s final menstrual period, most commonly only identifiable after one year without menstruation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is only after one year without a period, that we can safely say that a women is in menopause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perimenopause refers to the phase prior to menopause when a women’s normal menstrual cycle of approximately 28 days starts to vary in length by seven or more days, but also includes the year after the final menstrual period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The average length of perimenopause is about four years, but it can last up to 10 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is slightly lower than in so-called "western" countries, where the average age is 51.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: From youth to senior years, women experience unique events – such as menstruation, menopause and for some, conception and childbirth." For many women menopause and perimenopause are just routine stages in life, with the only physical manifestation being the absence, or a reduction in, menstruation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, for some women it is a completely different story.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While every woman’s experience is different, menopause can have a sometimes severe and debilitating impact on a woman’s: physical and mental health; her overall enjoyment of life; the quality of her relationships with her partner, children and family; her ability to take part in social, recreational and professional activities; and her participation in the work force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For example, for some women menopause and perimenopause can be accompanied by: irregular, or unusually light or heavy, menstrual periods; hot flushes, night sweats and sleep problems, including fatigue and insomnia; mood changes, including anxiety, anger, grief and depression; urinary tract infections and urinary incontinence; loss of bone density and an increased risk of osteoporosis and stress fractures; rapid weight change; an increase in LDL cholesterol and a decrease in HDL cholesterol; heart disease, hypertension and heart palpitations; muscular and joint pain; itchy skin; dry mouth and trouble concentrating or remembering words or facts, or "brain fog".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The study also noted that the most commonly reported symptoms included muscular and joint pain, sleep disturbances, physical and mental exhaustion and hot flushes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is encouraging to see that Singapore has already introduced several initiatives to support individuals facing mental health challenges, including the People's Action Party Mental Health Group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: An often-overlooked aspect of mental health is, however, the impact of menopause and perimenopause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A February 2024 study from Cardiff University found that women undergoing perimenopause often experience a wide range of neurological and psychiatric symptoms, yet these issues remain trivialised and misunderstood in both medical and workplace settings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The same study reported that the connection between menopause and mental health challenges is frequently under-recognised and insufficiently addressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Menopause and perimenopause can also have a significant impact on a women’s workforce participation, productivity and retirement planning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A 2024 Australian Senate standing committee inquiry into issues related to menopause and perimenopause reported that menopause and perimenopause contribute to a reduction in performance at work; hesitancy or inability to take on additional or higher roles and responsibilities; working part-time or less hours than preferred; leaving the workforce earlier than planned; concerns about future career goals and prospects; reduced personal savings, including superannuation; increased financial stress and distress; and increased financial reliance on partners or family members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Results of a 2018 survey by the Irish Congress of Trade Unions showed that while many women faced significant workplace challenges due to menopause, there was little support available to address these issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While it is difficult to know the proportion of these women that are retiring due specifically to the impacts of menopause, anecdotal evidence presented at a recent Australian Senate Inquiry into menopause suggests a strong link.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Another study by the UK Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found that two-thirds, or 67% of working women between the ages of 40 and 60 with menopausal symptoms said the symptoms had a mostly negative impact on them at work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I expect that it would be unusual for a woman in Singapore or, indeed, anywhere in the world to comfortably disclose to her employer that is struggling emotionally or physically due to menopause or perimenopause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My concern with this argument is that if we know that menopause and perimenopause increase the number of days that women may require medical leave, then it seems inequitable to offer women the same number of days of medical leave as men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Menopause and perimenopause are uniquely female-only issues and, just as women require more restrooms in the workplace than men, perhaps they also need more leave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Close the Gap Scotland highlighted the correlation between menopause and workplace equality, and I quote, "The impact of menopause at work is interwoven with the impact of workplace gender inequality, and the power imbalance between women and men in the workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As men age in the workplace, this is associated with perceived increased status and credibility, however it is the opposite for women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is a result of gender norms and inequality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Older women in the workplace also face an increasing challenge of ‘sandwich caring’ – providing care for both elderly parents and grandchildren".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Dealing with these events can, at the best of times, be stressful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, the addition of even one or two of the more common side effects of menopause and perimenopause can make coping with some of the more routine or predictable aspects of life substantially harder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Talking openly about menopause is often associated with shame, embarrassment and misunderstanding, making it difficult for women to comfortably seek reliable and accurate information and support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Menopause is also tied to gendered ageism, as it is often seen as a negative bodily process that reflects societal and organisational attitudes toward ageing and mature women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This position is echoed by Prof Susan Davis, Director of the Monash University Women’s Health Research Programme in Australia, who, in June 2024, commented, and I quote, “There has been no quality, cross-sectional data about menopause collected in the last 10 years in any country in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We do not really know collectively the voice of women.” Without reliable data, understanding the health, social and professional impacts of menopause in Singapore will remain difficult.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In the Senate inquiry I referenced earlier, women spoke about medical practitioners having a limited understanding of the symptoms of menopause and perimenopause and the associated difficulty in getting a reliable diagnosis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Some women also spoke about the lack of awareness among medical practitioners as leading to symptoms of menopause and perimenopause, particularly in younger women, being diagnosed as being stress related.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This includes not only biological differences, such as age of onset of symptoms, but also community perceptions and responses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Ethnographies of menopause have shown that all cultures attach both positive and negative meanings to ageing and menopause, demonstrating the need for a more nuanced and empathetic approach to this stage in a woman's life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by Prof Gita Mishra from the School of Public Health, University of Queensland, in some cultures, menopause is simply not spoken about publicly, whereas in others, reaching menopause is, and I quote, "Associated with an experience of enhanced wisdom or becoming more revered." Regardless of the pros and cons of such differences, there is little available data on culturally sensitive and relevant approaches to understanding and responding to menopause and perimenopause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, including information about menopause and perimenopause in the health or science health curriculum would assist to normalise the subject and prepare girls for this inevitable life stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It may also assist to increase awareness and understanding among boys and young men and to break down existing gender-based misunderstandings and stereotypes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to acknowledge the excellent work being done by several local social service agencies, with a special mention to Surety Singapore who inform and support women navigating menopause and, in November 2024, will be hosting Menopause Festival 2024.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, I need to acknowledge that I drew inspiration from several initiatives either in place or currently under consideration across the globe, most notably Australia and the UK, both of whom have taken considerable steps in progressing systemic understanding and response to menopause and perimenopause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I also took into consideration the White Paper on Singapore Women's Development, published by SAWA, in collaboration with PPIS, AWARE, SCWO and Tsao Foundation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I agree with many of the points raised by Assoc Prof Razwana.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She shared about the health impact of menopause on women and how we can address this impact with training of healthcare providers, research into contributing factors and management, public education and social support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will now address her points in my speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some may experience significant impact to their health and well-being, beyond the more common symptoms, such as hot flushes, night sweats and insomnia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is because as the protective effects of oestrogen on the heart diminish, this can potentially lead to an increased risk of heart disease and stroke.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Changes in metabolism during menopause can also result in weight gain, particularly around the abdomen, which may increase the risk of diabetes and other metabolic disorders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana also highlighted that women undergoing menopause can experience changes in mood, which can impact their mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is important to note that while these health impacts of concern, they can be managed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Regular check-ups, a healthy lifestyle, including exercise, eating well and finding ways to relax can help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Simple things like using moisturisers for dryness and choosing appropriate clothing to manage hot flushes can also make a difference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For significant symptoms impacting quality of life, women should see their doctor to explore suitable interventions to manage the impact on both physical and mental health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We agree that educating our medical students and medical practitioners on menopause is important and we have been doing so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Postgraduate family medicine programmes, such as the Family Medicine residency programme and the Graduate Diploma in Family Medicine include training on common women's health conditions, including menopause, in the curriculum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Professional bodies, such as the College of Family Physicians Singapore also run skills courses on a variety of topics relevant to primary care practice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These efforts enable our primary care doctors to be a source of support to women in managing the health issues that may arise during this life transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Under Healthier SG, the relationship between the primary care doctor and enrollee is central.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Women who are experiencing menopausal symptoms can inform their primary care doctor, who would be well placed to assess the symptoms, the patient's needs and make recommendations on further management.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Member also mentioned KKH and the KK Menopause Centre.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This multi-specialty practice comprising of gynaecology, family medicine, dermatology and mental health specialists, has been trained to support a range of needs of women with menopausal-related health issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mental health services are also available in various care settings to identify women who may be experiencing psychological symptoms and provide interventions when required.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Research into menopause would provide more insight into how it affects women's overall health and well-being, and enable better ways to manage menopause symptoms and its impact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Issues studied include the associations between menopause and age-related health issues, such as osteoporosis and sleep disturbances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The research team plans to conduct follow-up studies and we look forward to further insights that the IWHP and other researchers can provide on women's health in general, as well as menopause specifically.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Women should not feel ashamed, embarrassed or misunderstood to speak openly about menopause.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As a society, we should work to remove the stigma surrounding menopause, and we are already taking steps to educate the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Reliable information on menopause can be found on HealthHub and the websites of our public healthcare institutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Education about menopause is important to help women understand what to expect and how to manage the changes to their body.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue to empower women to approach menopause with confidence and make informed decisions about their health and well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To truly enhance women's well-being during menopause, we must address not only the physical symptoms, but also the psychological and social impacts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This includes combating stigma, promoting open dialogue and ensuring that women have access to accurate information and supportive resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Civil society and community organisations are well-placed to participate in this effort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They can play a critical role in providing support for women and creating platforms for the public in general to discuss and better understand issues surrounding menopause.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, many women who are going through menopause are concurrently taking on caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We support caregivers to balance caregiving while pursuing their aspirations and caring for their own health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are enhancing options to make childcare and eldercare more accessible, affordable and available, for example, by scaling up childcare and eldercare capacity, and providing multiple layers of financial support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These, in tandem with other moves to support women at work, will support women to better balance their responsibilities, and their own health and well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana also spoke about suggestions for MOE and MOM, touching on educating people about menopause in schools and workplace policies that better support women with menopause.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In MOE's Sexuality Education and Science curriculum, students learn about menstrual health in women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Primary 5 students learn about the physiological changes that occur during puberty, such as menstruation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Students are also educated on human reproduction and issues related to menstrual health in Lower Secondary Science and Upper Secondary Biology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On workplace policies, women who experience severe menopausal symptoms can already seek subsidised medical treatment at Public Healthcare Institutions, and take sick leave to rest and recover, just like any other medical need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There have been calls for menopause leave or reproductive leave in other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Most recently in the UK, the government rejected a call by the Women and Equalities Committee to conduct a trial of menopause leave last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Like the UK, our preferred approach is to support women to remain in the workforce and be well-supported at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, flexible work arrangements (FWAs) can help employees with other medical conditions to balance the care needs for their condition with work responsibilities, including women experiencing perimenopause or menopause.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We encourage employers to use these Guidelines to engage their employees in conversations and find mutually beneficial arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government will continue to work with tripartite partners to foster supportive workplaces, so that all employees can participate fully at work while managing their own personal needs, such as family responsibilities and medical conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government is committed to building a society where all Singaporeans have full and equal opportunities to flourish and achieve their aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Civil society and community organisations have an important part to play as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Together, by providing education and support, we hope to take a whole of society approach to enable women to navigate this transition with confidence, maintaining their well-being and full participation in all aspects of life.
